items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家欧马尔·索萨在疫情隔离与婚姻变故期间，受邀于意大利法齐奥利钢琴厂音乐厅进行两小时无脚本独奏即兴，后以人声片段、打击乐、循环、实地录音与拾得声音进行少量混音处理。作品以独奏钢琴为轴心，采用拨弦、抚弦等内钢琴技法，扩展琴体共鸣；即兴遵循“不重复”的信念，首遍演奏即被视为灵魂的自然声音。索萨表明拒绝风格标签，将古巴传统与普遍主义精神探索融入声响，试图以带泛音的低频共鸣连接“海底轮”，让音乐成为面向迷失人性的修行路径。

items.body: Of the many things that make albums featuring John Butcher unique, I believe the most outstanding characteristic is not that he likes to play at unusual venues (caves, water reservoirs, oil tanks…), but rather the fact that every ensemble he plays with is so diverse and incomparable that it allows the listener to hear many different facets of his playing. In an interview with Brad Rose, Butcher said that when improvising, he likes to hear the musician behind the instrument, though it’s not important to him to hear the musicians putting themselves in the spotlight - on the contrary, he tends to seek subtlety. In general, he looks for musicians who have already developed a personal musical style and their own way of playing - something that truly feels like their own. It is therefore almost inevitable that the various ensembles he selects based on these criteria will possess a unique dynamic and sonic world. One of last year’s best albums was RARE , John Butcher’s duo with French pianist Sophie Agnel, with whom he had been playing quite frequently over the last few years. I especially liked their improvisational rigor and the relaxed, varied, and aleatoric moments. On RARE , I considered the pauses in the music to be the central element; on foams & mesh , it’s different, mainly due to Pascal Niggenkemper (bass) and Ståle Liavik Solberg (drums), because the two of them fill those gaps. Solberg, with whom Butcher has played since 2015 in many kinds of combinations, permeates the improvisation with his bone-dry and at times almost esoteric style, for example when he uses extended materials (especially in the quiet passages of the first track). This is complemented by Agnel’s trills, which she plays from inside the piano. Butcher contributes very delicate bird calls here, while Niggenkemper subtly saws at the very low strings of his bass. It feels as though one is listening to the goings-on in the courtyard of a Tibetan monastery. This can be heard around the 20-mark of the first, significantly longer improvisation on foam & mesh. Such passages contrast with highly expressive moments, in which the rhythm section performs in a demanding and driving manner, but Butcher remains unflappable and employs his entire repertoire - guttural sounds, chirps, tremolos, circular breathing, serial/repetitive patterns, etc. - with casual ease. Only at the end of the track Agnel’s clusters and crescendos, Niggenkemper’s alienated drones and Solberg’s accentuated interceptions tempt him into vibrato-heavy phrases. The album was recorded at the artacts festival in St. Johann/Austria in 2024 and in the first part of the encore the musicians showcase extended playing techniques, with Niggenkemper and Agnel holding the improvisation together by a somber drone. Then the bass and piano shift imperceptibly into their normal registers, and the piece grows denser, builds in intensity, becoming louder and more concentrated - like a tornado - before dissolving perfectly. foam & mesh is an extraordinary album, the band is a superb match. They have played only three concerts so far and I think I’m not the only one who hopes that there will be more to come. foam & mesh is available as a CD and as a download. You can buy and listen to the album on the label’s website: https://sluchaj.bandcamp.com/album/foam-mesh foam & mesh by B:A:N:S BAND: Sophie Agnel / John Butcher / Pascal Niggenkemper / Ståle Liavik Solberg Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是John Butcher与Sophie Agnel、Pascal Niggenkemper、Ståle Liavik Solberg组成的四重奏现场录音，展现了自由即兴中罕见的动态平衡。乐评指出，与前作RARE以留白为核心不同，foams & mesh由贝斯与鼓手填补空隙，形成更密集的即兴对话。作品在极简段落与高能爆发间切换：萨克斯的鸟鸣、钢琴内部的颤音、低音提琴的低音锯弦与干燥鼓击交织，营造出类似寺院庭院的冥想氛围；随后又在打击乐驱动下转入紧张亢奋的集体即兴，最终以渐强的龙卷风般音势收束。录音来自2024年艺术节现场，曲目包含加演段落，展示了乐手对扩展技法的娴熟运用与临场结构的精密把控，是一张具有鲜明声响探索色彩的自由爵士专辑。

items.body: Label: Calligram Records, 2026 Personnel - Geof Bradfield: tenor and soprano saxophone, bass clarinet; Ben Goldberg: clarinet, contra alto clarinet; Myra Melford: piano; Dana Hall: drums. What a wonderful time I had listening to this fantastic bass-less quartet, whose powerful avant-garde jazz captivates from start to finish. Recorded live at Chicago’s legendary Green Mill, Open or Close gathers compositions from all four members—saxophonist Geof Bradfield, clarinetist Ben Goldberg, pianist Myra Melford, and drummer Dana Hall—who, having crossed musical paths before in several contexts, make a remarkable debut as a group here. Ornette Coleman’s “ Open or Close ” is the stunning opener, showcasing a memorable eight-note riff that gradually evolves into staccato activity resembling rhythmic shocks of vibrant color. Initially, Melford constructs melodies around that riff, with Hall’s percussive driving force as her sole support. Goldberg’s sinewy clarinet phrasing also prompts quick responses from the drummer and effective comping from Melford; then Bradfield offers an earthy, motivic solo packed with tension and release before the theme returns. Melford’s “ A Line With a Mind of Its Own ”, inspired by American painter and sculptor Cy Twombly, is built over an exquisite scale, patiently expressed as a chamber-jazz concerto with moderate snare-drum effervescence, accelerations, and mounting intensity. The pianist also contributes the adventurous “ The Kitchen ”. Goldberg also brings two contrasting yet extremely effective compositions: “ Study of the Blues ” is definitely not your standard model within the genre, but rather a slightly dissonant exploratory piece with a lot of interesting things going on; “ Three Ingredients ”, on the other hand, is a bop-inflected piece centered on an expeditious figure. Starting as a conversation between contra-alto and bass clarinets, the tune evolves into a sort of avant-garde ragtime. The groove-forward standouts are marvelous to witness, and they provide a setting in which each musician’s distinct personality emerges naturally. Bradfield’s “ No Brand ”, a dedication to South African pianist Abdullah Ibrahim, flows with a feel-good, six-beat contra-alto clarinet groove, hi-hat buoyancy, and melodic discernment fueled by the parallel motion created by soprano sax and piano. During Goldberg’s beautifully articulated statement, there is no disruption to the groove in the lower register as he and the pianist switch roles. By the end, Bradfield and Melford mirror each other in thrilling interplay. Another dedication to a South African musician, bassist Johnny Dyani, comes with “ Lonely Flowers ”, a piece Dyani wrote himself and first recorded in 1978. These African scents also bring a touch of Sun Ra’s exoticism into play, and I love Bradfield’s fierce improvisational spirit here on tenor. Brimming with creative ideas, Open or Close has no weak tracks, with each one evoking thoughtful moods and sonic stimulation. These four musicians reveal exceptional musical capabilities, and their collective effort comes highly recommended. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Open or Close ► 03 - No Brand ► 04 - Study of the Blues ► 06 - Lonely Flowers
items._cn_summary: 这张由萨克斯、单簧管、钢琴与鼓组成的无贝斯四重奏现场专辑，以芝加哥Green Mill为背景，展现了当代前卫爵士的丰富面向。开场曲改编自Ornette Coleman的同名作品，以标志性的八音动机逐步演化为富有冲击力的跳跃节奏；Melford的钢琴写作兼具抒情线条与冒险精神，Goldberg的管乐演奏在细腻与粗粝间游走。专辑涵盖类似室内乐质感的渐进式作品、带有波普元素的即兴段落，以及向Abdullah Ibrahim和Johnny Dyani致敬的非洲律动篇章，在无贝斯的配置中通过管乐低音区与鼓的精密互动构建出独特的和声基座。四位音乐家均贡献作品，风格跨度从略不协和的探索到前卫拉格泰姆，整体保持高密度创意与即兴张力。

items.album: 『水野修孝：電子音楽全集』前衛芸術の鬼才が〈大音量で再生しなければならない〉と指示した“怒りの日”を収録
items.tags: クラシック 現代音楽 intoxicate 2026 August クラシック 現代音楽 # リイシュー クラシック 水野修孝
items.excerpt: 日本の前衛芸術の鬼才・水野修孝の電子音楽を集成したCDがリリースされた。中でも“怒りの日”と題されたコンクレート作品は〈この作品は大音量で再生しなければならない〉という作曲者自身の指示が残されていることで知られる。去る6月、私とスリーシェルズはこの作品を文字通り大音量で再生するリスニングイベントを開催。当日はタンノイで普段の約3倍、100dB近い爆音で再生した。それはまさに音の斬撃そのもの。音が波であることを改めて実感すると共に、この作品はイヤホン等で聴くものではなく、大きなスピーカーを通して全身で浴びるように体感してこそ真価を発揮するのだと確信した。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑汇集了日本前卫艺术家水野修孝的电子音乐作品，其中核心曲目《怒りの日》是一首具象音乐作品，作曲者明确指示必须以大音量播放。乐评人记述了与三只贝壳（Three Shells）合作举办的大音量试听活动，通过Tannoy音箱以接近100dB的声压级播放，音量约为平时的三倍。现场体验被描述为“声音的斩击”，让人重新意识到声音作为波动的物理本质。乐评强调，此类作品不适合用耳机聆听，而应通过大型扬声器让声波包裹全身，以身体感受其冲击力。水野修孝的创作融合了前卫艺术观念与电子声音技术，在编排上具有强烈的实验性和身体性，是理解日本当代实验音乐的重要样本。

items.body: Drone has an incredible tonal range. With sounds that range from calm to abrasive, drone can soothe or unsettle, like the distance between a refrigerator hum and an attack copter. These albums not only reflect the sounds that flow through our bodies, perceptible or not, but the hum, buzz and noise of everyday life. Earth’s empty aural spaces are being filled in slowly by sound, from subsonic frequency to passing plane. Those who work in this field underline the musical aspects of drone: subtle shifts, undulations, tension and release. Turning the intrusive into the sonically desired is yet another form of reclamation. Our cover image is from Marta Salogni & Stefano Pilia‘s Phren on Maple Death, covered below. As always, our discussion of drone begins with the amazing Room40 label, whose roster focuses on drone yet is in no way restricted to it. We’ll be listing all of the imprint’s fall announcements here, including those of Someone Good, since Lawrence English has done such a fine job with advance publicity and it looks tidy! The first is a re-release of David Shea‘s I, originally on Sub Rosa; the Zorn-influenced album still sounds fresh and raucous (September 2). Next on the schedule is Werner Defeldecker + Eliad Wagner‘s Fray Field; readers may recall Dafeldecker’s Fathom Tidea with Lawrence English from earlier this year. This improvised album of double bass, synth and guitar is a whole different beast (September 11). Jannis Anastasakis and Peter Knight follow with Feather, a two-and-a-half-hour performance distilled to 32 minutes, light as air (September 18). The month ends with Hannes Strobl‘s Resonance IBK, an immersive five-part piece that blends field recordings of mountain and valley with complementary, drone-like music, and Prime Frequencies from mHz, who brought us 2024’s Material Prosody. The latter album, available in code and web-based formats, contains 47 investigations of sine waves and their relationship to prime numbers (September 25).   Room40’s October slate begins with Andrew Tuttle & Darren Cross‘ AT/DC (no, that’s not a typo)! This warm guitar and banjo set is enhanced by reverb and synthesizer, reminiscent of Rain Drinkers (October 2). Winter comes early with Philip Samartzis & Michael Vorfeld‘s Atmospheric Pressure, an acoustic reflection of a 36-hour Antarctic blizzard (October 9). Matt Rösner‘s Lost Meridians follows, described as “music to pause to,” reflecting the peace of open prairies and wide, unpolluted skies (October 16). Yann Novak‘s Discontinuity is a remixed response to Continuity, as well as a commentary on “deteriorating conditions in the U.S.” (October 16). Bruno Duplant investigates the nature of erosion through sound, offering l’usure du socle stable du monde, a two-part study meant to be experienced as a single piece (October 23). Steven Hess + Rutger Zuydervelt follow Re:collecting exactly a decade later with Re:construct. Times have changed, but there’s always a place for hope (October 30).   Maple Death continues its fabulous run with another box set produced in conjunction with Opale. Phren is a collaborative effort from Marta Salogni & Stefano Pilia, introduced with an eleven-minute hymn that turns out to be the album’s most sedate selection, a worthy closer after the weight of the preceding tracks. The cover art is only the beginning; more of Sarah Mazzetti’s illustrations lie within (October 2). zakè‘s Tide Requiem for the Low Sea is a beauty to behold, available on increasingly rare picture disc vinyl. The music is like the end of summer, the art like an invitation to extend the season (September 2). The Sirens begins with the sound of an observatory door being opened. Geologist & Kyle Simon‘s music twinkles and shines, like a planetarium score or the biography of starlight (Outside Time, October 16). Calum Builder plays a reconstructed Copenhagen pipe organ on Although Changed, I Arise the Same, accompanied by vocal fragments culled from the Psalms. This results is a double reconstruction of faith and sound (thanatosis, September 25).   Tehran-born, Berlin-based Ava Rasti‘s No One Knows How Wild the Wind Blows is a harrowing reflection on current conditions in Iran. Aslan Mohammadpour‘s video for the title track starts as a benign home video before literally pulling back the curtain (FatCat / 130701, October 30). Falling into dark ambient-drone territory with titles such as “Circle of Black Candles,” Ajna‘s Mysterium Tremendum can’t wait for sunset. On this album, darkness is meant to evoke transcendence as well as fear (Winter-Light, September 4). Eric Angelo Bessel‘s Illusion of an Inland Ocean is murky, dark and mysterious, a reflection of everything from the ocean depths to the depths of the soul (Lore City Music, October 30). Seven bagpipe players and three basin players create an enveloping sound on Erwan Keravec‘s There will be no miracles here; check this video for insight on the performance. The organic sound borders on the otherworldly (Buda Musique, October 16). Rachel Shearer honors the earth and the Māori concept of whakapapa on Te Oro o Te Ao, as Maori vocals give way to a massive wall of field recordings and lead to a peaceful denouement (Thin Wrist Recordings, October 9). Falsetto singing, harmonium and cassette are the hallmarks of KKKAAARRREEENNNIIINNNAAA, an album as wild as its spelling bee title, courtesy of Charlemagne Palestine / Oren Ambarchi / Daniel O’Sullivan (Black Truffle, September 10).   Kai Niggemann‘s Climate and Violence began as music for the theatre performance “Denkraum der Utopien,” and has been updated and tweaked for this release. Since then, global climate change has only accelerated, and threatens to increase exponentially. The morphing music reflects shifts in atmospheric conditions and long-range forecasts (WAF80 Music, September 25). Giulio Aldinucci‘s Materia treats sound as matter that can be sculpted; the pieces feel like clay, molded and remolded, resisting their final forms (Karlrecords, September 18). Haarvöl‘s Overflowed Shelters is a direct commentary on recent events, highlighted by the harrowing first single, “Perpetual Ruins (a lament for Gaza).” The music reflects a slow-motion genocide, a horror from which many turn away, but that demands to be seen and confronted. There’s no escape in this music, nor should there be (Moving Furniture, September 26).   Thomas Brinkmann‘s GETGETGET is a single piece in two parts, born of a live performance. Listening is like traveling through the various permutations of drone, thin to thick, soft to loud, with percussion serving as additional texture (Editions Mego, October 23). A “diverse ecology of machines” is used on Ben Carey‘s INVENTIONS, which at times sounds like a cathedral tower and at other times a factory floor (Hospital Hill, September 14). Markus Solid creates immersive atmospheres by combining drone and electronics. Elastic Embrace is as mutable as its title, bent forward and back, refusing to break (Rhizome, September 25). ARROWOUNDS‘ Fludiic Time Cathedral is dark and mysterious, as one might expect from the artist who brought us In the Octopus Pond. The style is gothic rock drenched in shoegaze timbres, removed from the ether while still dripping, a worthy finale for Lost Tribe Sound’s Moss & Melee series (September 25). Richard Allen
items._genre: drone / experimental / ambient / electronic / field recording
items._cn_summary: 该乐评集中介绍了多家厂牌在秋季发行的 drone 专辑，尤其以 Room40 及其子厂牌为主。这些作品从双低音提琴、合成器与吉他的即兴碰撞，到两小时半演出压缩为三十二分钟的轻盈之声，再到融合山区与山谷实地录音的沉浸式五乐章，以及基于正弦波与素数关系的四十七项声音研究，展示了 drone 在音色、结构与素材上的广阔可能性。部分作品还涉及对南极暴风雪、草原天空等自然环境的声学回应，或以声音探讨美国社会状况的恶化。文章强调 drone 既能让日常噪音转化为听觉渴望，也能在极简变化中制造张力与释然，整体呈现了实验声响与氛围叙事并重的多元面貌。

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — I tend to root for the underdogs, and so The King of Limbs is the first Radiohead album I'm properly reviewing as I work my way through the catalogue. And, frankly, this one does have me puzzled.This is the album that seems to land near the bottom of the list for many Radiohead fans. It's their eighth studio album, and apparently it's the one you're supposed to approach with lowered expectations. Yet when I glance at the Wikipedia page, I find something rather different: The King of Limbs was named among the best albums of 2011 by a number of major music publications, and it went on to receive five Grammy nominations, including Best Alternative Music Album.So here I was thinking, Gosh, it must be too weird or weak? And it's a funny thing, too, that expectations can spoil a gift?or, depending on the circumstances, make it even better.But speaking frankly, I tend to like just about everything I hear from this band and its individual members. There's something about Radiohead that can always draws me in, and I think they set an example of artistic integrity that any band could and should learn from. "Wildness and mutations" were a couple of Thom Yorke's choice words describing it.The King of Limbs, it turns out, isn't overly grounded in the day-to-day. It's a subtle, glitchy, laid-back and pensive album. It unfolds like a pleasant daydream, scattered with illogical bits and flashes, hiding all sorts of secret messages and meanings. It's a trippy, sometimes ethereal, relaxing ride into an alternate timeline that Thom Yorke and friends have cooked up.The percussion?often looped?is peculiar throughout. The loops in a couple of the songs (1 and 4) remind me of riding the streetcars and subways of Toronto: that mesmerizing clickety-clack of the car rattling along while people and traffic carry on outside, the whole city moving around you as you gaze through the window.'Codex' was one of my favourites on the disc. It sits and fits so nicely among the rest of the songs. It's melancholic and soulful, with a slowly played, affected piano that moves along with a gentle kick drum, pumping like a heartbeat. Hard to believe they chose brass to adorn the song, but it works perfectly, thanks to the warmth and tenderness with which it's played and mixed. Then, near the end, the song briefly transforms, introducing an otherworldly orchestration paired with the most uncanny bloom of electronic noise?something that feels like invisible audio static cling.Moments like these are what make this album.Thom Yorke is a vocalist I find hard to quantify. I like his singing... a lot. Maybe I love it. He always sounds convincing, and somehow sells whatever it is he's meditating on. There's a fragility to his voice, too, and some kind of persona he embodies when he performs.Maybe that's it: he performs. He is really into it when he sings. He doesn't just deliver the melody or the lyrics; he channels something. There's a sense that he's inhabiting whatever emotional space the song occupies, rather than simply singing about it.For me, 'Little by Little' has that trademark stamp of a Radiohead composition: a simple, vanilla-flavoured guitar tone paired with low and mid notes ascending the guitar neck in that customarily wiggly way, teasing their way in and out of musical keys and defying logic to just the right degree. All the while, a crowded ensemble of various percussion instruments blip, shake and busily ticky-tick along. Refreshing!'Lotus Flower' feels like a jam, propelled by happiness-inducing handclaps. (I just can't imagine any other use for handclaps than to express joy.) I love how they use the most unsuspecting synthesizer tones to animate the chorus. They remind me of an old, weird plastic keyboard my cousins had in their basement back in the '70s, sitting next to their toy-like record player with records like 'Super Gold Hits' by K-Tel.My least favourite song melody-wise is 'Give Up the Ghost', but its lyrical sentiment redeems it somewhat for me. I've always liked the image it creates in my mind of coming home after a long day and turning to a spouse, a sibling, or a parent for an embrace when you're completely exhausted and ready to just give in.The final track is an appropriate send-off: 'Separator' is repetitive but starts to bloom and take off and soar a little after it's bleak beginning. "Wake me up, will you wake me up" No, Thom. We are enjoying the ride just fine, thank-you very much, and we should both just linger here a little longer... Prog dog album score: 4 bones out of 5.

items._cn_summary: 乐评认为这张专辑被许多乐迷低估，但实际获得多项格莱美提名。音乐呈现微妙、故障感、悠闲而沉思的气质，如同散落着不合逻辑片段的白日梦，隐藏着各种秘密信息。循环打击乐贯穿全篇，其节奏令人联想到多伦多街车与地铁的咔嗒声。歌曲《Codex》是亮点，忧郁而深情，缓慢的钢琴伴随如心跳般的轻柔底鼓，铜管编配温暖妥帖，结尾处突然转化为超凡的管弦乐与诡异的电子噪音。Thom Yorke的演唱具有说服力，声音脆弱而投入，仿佛在演绎某种角色。整体上，专辑以松弛而迷幻的方式构建出一个另类时间线，值得反复聆听。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — A couple of details set Starless and Bible Black apart from its contemporaries of the 1970s. The first was the departure of percussionist Jamie Muir, who left for a monastery after the recording of Larks' Tongues in Aspic, leaving Bill Bruford in charge of percussion. The second was the contribution of lyrics by Richard Palmer-James (Supertramp's original guitarist and a friend of John Wetton); he penned the words for "The Great Deceiver" and "Lament," which critique societal commercialism and fame, while "The Night Watch" serves as a study of the Rembrandt painting of the same name, and "The Mincer" appears to be a piece of free association. The album title, Starless and Bible Black, references a work by the poet Dylan Thomas. This speaks to the literary aspect, a significant source of inspiration that was very much in vogue at the time, though sadly, it has increasingly become a relic of that era today. Musically, the band, who had been improvising more and more during tours since the Islands era, incorporated several live improvisations into the album. What is remarkable is that, while these pieces clearly originated as improvisations, they are so well-structured that they possess a narrative arc, to use a literary metaphor, featuring an introduction, a climax, and a resolution. They offer a dramatic progression that tells a story: a composition with profound meaning that leaves the spirit fulfilled upon listening.A different concept infused the album, a different tempo: faster, more aggressive, and stripped of the lengthy preludes of the past. The bass and drum foundation was more prominent, and John Wetton stood out as both a great vocalist and a superb bassist. "The Great Deceiver" accelerates until the song suddenly begins to deconstruct, as if its parts were being dissected for minute analysis, a formula Fripp would further perfect in the future. And just like that...as abruptly as it begins, it ends...and "Lament" begins, full of calm and mystery.Wetton's voice is perfect for the kind of music Fripp was composing, music that was alive and evolving, changing from album to album; sometimes it would even change from concert to concert, without waiting for a recording to be made. David Cross's violin was the perfect companion... until the bass began to slice through the air, fracturing it, and Bruford, joined by Fripp, followed suit, corrupting and darkening the melody, just as Wetton's voice shifted to match the change, turning more aggressive. Then... the rhythm shifted once more, accelerating to a frenetic pace that the bass, drums, and guitar all tracked. Wetton's bass was funky and deeply groovy, while Bruford's drumming was all over the place, at times a cannonball, at others a machine gun, an entire arsenal at the service of the composition; he knew exactly when to hit the gas during the final coda and when to slam on the brakes, allowing silence to reclaim the stage, a true master of timing and its application."We'll Let You Know" is the first of those improvisations that are partly improvised yet don't quite seem like it; the opening, which never quite kicks into gear and seems to have no clear direction, actually reveals itself to be a perfectly crafted introduction for what follows. Once again, Wetton amazes with his unique feel and sensitivity, laying down a funk groove while Fripp sends musical streamers spiraling through the air... and when Bruford joins in, the whole thing explodes; without a doubt, Flea listened to this, alongside Funkadelic and Sly Stone, when composing the Red Hot Chili Peppers' Blood Sugar Sex Magik."The Night Watch", much like "Book of Saturday" was on the previous album, is the heart of Starless & Bible Black. With its Eastern atmosphere steeped in Japanese tradition (marking Fripp's first foray into that culture) and Wetton's sweet, relaxed, and wise vocals, the track achieves a magical "eclipse of the sun," driven by phrasing and Fripp's accompanying guitar work that have since become legendary. This is part of the band's magic, a quality that was never truly lost, as evidenced by "Matte Kudasai" in the 1980s lineup and "One Time" in the 1990s.During the recording of "Trio" at the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam, a piece driven entirely by Mellotron and violin, Bruford waited for the right moment to join in; however, deeming the performance perfect as it was, he never actually entered the song. The rest of the band considered this "lack of intervention" so precise, adding as much to the composition as if he had played, that it made him a composer of the piece "in his absence," just as much as they were through their actual participation.That tribal, and even almost playful air that The Mincer can possess vanishes as soon as the two concluding pieces (I'll call them "Suites") begin; they are improvisations akin to highways with a clearly marked, signposted route, and even when they ventured into dark jungles, the musicians knew where they were going and reached their destination, however much one might have doubted it at times. Starless and Bible Black begins gradually, so subtly, in fact, that one could say silence itself initiates it. Then, that guitar that sets everything ablaze emerges, like a distant alarm or a prehistoric wail. The Mellotron plays a pivotal role in crafting the album's universe; it is a descent into the underworld, where the bass and the impeccably precise drums only serve to heighten the tension. That Mellotron, paired with the bass, could almost pioneer a form of progressive funk, a fusion of the two genres unfolding beneath a musical landscape that is incredibly dense and complex."Fracture" is the album's other gem, the discovery that would serve as the cornerstone for the creation of Red. Fripp's counterpoints launch a highly distinctive opening melody; once revealed, it recedes, beginning a process of retreat and decomposition into its constituent parts. It is a symphony in which every member of the quartet has a role to play, both when they appear and when they vanish, like an act of sleight of hand. Bruford hints at what is to follow, albeit in a chamber-music style, before gradually building a "crescendo" worthy of high dramatic suspense. The momentum is occasionally slowed by the violin until the quartet suddenly surges forward in unison, fusing into a single entity; they stretch the main melody like modeling clay, molding it into various shapes and playing with it, yet never losing sight of the ultimate goal, even as parallel paths deliberately prolong the tension leading up to that final resolution. Wetton matches Fripp's intensity, with Cross and Bruford providing support as the pitch rises ever higher... until only the distorted guitar remains, left hesitating in the wake of the successfully executed "fracture." Everything was set for the next step, the final step, and the time for doubt was over.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑将现场即兴素材精心编排为具有起承转合的叙事性结构，段落间呈现戏剧化的推进与解构。歌词层面引入迪伦·托马斯与伦勃朗画作等文学意象，批判商业社会与名声崇拜，赋予作品深厚的文化指涉。音乐上贝斯与鼓的律动更为突出，约翰·韦顿的演唱和演奏兼具力量与细腻，比尔·布鲁福德的打击乐在爆发与留白之间精准切换，整体速度更快、攻击性更强，同时保留了即兴中罕见的严密组织感。专辑值得聆听之处在于它模糊了即兴与作曲的边界，让每一次声响变化都服务于整体叙事，展现了乐队在七十年代中期独特的创作路径。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are many points where the style chosen by Mohini Dey touches upon the traditions of the 70s, both the virtuosity displayed on the bass, reminiscent of a great like Stanley Clarke, and that cosmic spirit that flowed not only through Return to Forever but also through the Mahavishnu Orchestra. That sort of jazz-style scat singing that opens "The Dey Way" is Konnakol, a form of vocal percussion from South India (also heard in Shakti with John McLaughlin); the 5-string slap bass gives it a punchy, defined sound, yet it isn't all sonic pyrotechnics, the music knows when to dial back the rhythm and calm the waters. What truly stands out is an abundance of hypnotic rhythm, complemented by Jonathan Mones's saxophone and bass lines that mimic the action of a sinuous defibrillator."Xtroverted Soul" features dissonant vocal harmonies that, in their ritualistic quality, truly recall the choral work of Zeuhl bands. Yet, it is a prime example of fusion at its best, with the guitar dancing in time to a perfectly integrated chorus that climbs ever higher in pitch, mirroring the saxophones. On "Whammy Award," one can hear keyboards as well as wind instruments, adding sonic variety, while her vocals are quite unconventional, reminiscent of Vinx, the soulful singer from Screaming Headless Torsos. And when she performs a bass solo, one can only conclude that Stanley Clarke's legacy is in good hands.The fusion with Indian rhythms makes the final result highly original, yet simultaneously recognizable and fresh, complemented by the spontaneity and joy she brings to her playing (much like Hiromi Uehara on the piano), which truly comes through in the music.When "Slappa Dey Bass" kicks in, the complexity of the arrangements clearly stems from the progressive nature of the compositions and the use of polyrhythms; as the trumpets and saxophones accelerate alongside the keyboards, the perfect atmosphere is created for her to improvise on the bass, displaying a style that quickly becomes familiar and establishes her own unique signature.With Joy, the band demonstrates its ability to craft a unique sound; the album feels gritty and street-smart yet sophisticated, simultaneously classic and modern. Echoes of Weather Report and Jaco Pastorius's style are audible, while "15 Steps Ahead" offers a more contemporary, electronic sound, featuring virtuosic performances of Eastern melodies and layered scales. At this point, the album engages in a nostalgic exercise, a nod to the past, as the chronological journey through history draws to a close, bringing us back to the postmodern present. Throughout, the playing remains organic and stirring."Uncle Dennis" is a highly syncopated funk track; with the horn section taking the lead, we hear the guest artist who gave the song its name: Dennis Chambers, a drummer known for his work with Mike Stern and Barbara Dennerlein, among others.The realm of possible sound is infinite; the final track, titled "Dad," pays homage to the very beginning of beginnings with a stripped-down, austere electric bass solo that speaks volumes.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以贝斯为核心，融合70年代爵士摇滚与印度传统节奏，展现出兼具炫技性与律动感的独特声音。开场曲运用南印度Konnakol声乐打击技法，配合五弦贝斯的击勾演奏，在密集节奏中保留呼吸空间。萨克斯与贝斯线条交织，营造出催眠般的律动；部分曲目加入不和谐人声和声，带有Zeuhl合唱的仪式感，同时吉他、键盘与管乐层层叠加，呈现前卫编曲的复杂性。专辑中段转向电子声响，东方旋律与分层音阶展现现代感，后段回归放克与融合传统，客座鼓手Dennis Chambers的加入强化了切分节奏。整体上，印度节奏与爵士摇滚的融合既保留历史脉络又具原创性，贝斯独奏延续了Stanley Clarke的遗产，演奏充满自发性的愉悦。

items.body: Nine years after “The Gag File”, Aaron Dilloway has a new solo album. The American experimental musician releases “No Skill Comedy Mind Reading” on Dais Records on 30 October 2026, his third proper solo LP and the first since 2017. Dilloway builds the record from 8-track tape loops, feedback-shrouded found sounds, field recordings and vocal improvisation, and it collects material drawn from close to a decade of solo work. No Skill Comedy Mind Reading by Aaron Dilloway Dilloway treats the album as the closing part of a set of three. He described the connection between them in the announcement, and he did so without separating the humour from the damage: “I almost feel like they’re kind of part of one piece. All three records are trying to find humor in the worst possible situations. Depending on who is listening and what their mindset is, they could be seen as funny or just horrifying, horrible records.” The sequence starts with “Modern Jester”, issued by his own Hanson Records in 2012, and runs through “The Gag File”, his first release for Dais Records in 2017. Eight tracks make up the album: “Raw Hyde”, “My Brain Has Finished Growing”, “Forced Auctioneer”, “Find A New Way To Laugh”, “Bring Me The Head Of The Unknown Comic”, “Possession Audition Tape”, “The Levitation Hacker” and “Supporting Actor (for Pieter & Phil)”. Dais Records has shared the first track, “Find A New Way To Laugh”, as official audio, and the album is available to pre-order. What shaped ‘No Skill Comedy Mind Reading’ Three reference points sit behind the record: the sound design of Alvin Lucier, Andy Milligan’s low-budget 1989 horror film “The Weirdo”, and the film composer Hugo Montenegro. Dilloway acquired a set of Montenegro’s belongings through a storage-unit auction, including notes from the composer’s early electronic experiments, and material from that find feeds several of the album’s more unsettled passages. The laughter running through “Bring Me The Head Of The Unknown Comic” nods sonically to Nurse With Wound and thematically to the paper-bag-headed 1970s American television comedian. Tape hiss is treated as material rather than as a defect. Dilloway traces that back to the cassettes he was given as a teenager, by the Misfits and Circle Jerks among others, on which the artifacts of repeated dubbing had become part of what he was hearing: “I am into the idea of building all of these layers and turning them into something else. Like when I play live, things can get harsher than my recorded music, and for this, I wanted to get that feeling, for these blasts to be loud, but a bit more subdued. That complete static sound, almost like you’re underwater.” The drone that opens the album comes from two Nepali sarangi bows rubbed against each other, an instrument Dilloway encountered during the period he spent living and recording in Nepal from late 2004. On the B-side, “Possession Audition Tape” cuts up phrases he reads from a book about an eighteenth-century French religious group given to public disruption. The closing “Supporting Actor (for Pieter & Phil)” is a synth and organ rhythm-machine piece derived from music he made for Pieter Schoolwerth and Phil Vanderhyden’s film “Supporting Actor”. The album took shape alongside other work. “This record has kind of consumed my head since I finished ‘The Gag File’ [2017]. At first, I was thinking it would be more of a pop record, but then the Lucrecia project kind of got that out of my system. It started to flow more like my live sets,” Dilloway said, referring to “Lucy & Aaron”, his 2021 album with Lucrecia Dalt. Aaron Dilloway tour dates 2026 Dilloway plays five US shows across September and October: 25 September 2026 – Los Angeles, CA, USA – Threshold 26 September 2026 – Cleveland, OH, USA – The Bent Mace 8 October 2026 – Chicago, IL, USA – Empty Bottle 9 October 2026 – Louisville, KY, USA – The B-Side 30 October 2026 – Pittsburgh, PA, USA – Woodstreet Galleries About Aaron Dilloway Aaron Dilloway was born on 13 May 1976 and grew up in Brighton, Michigan. As a teenager he began going to house shows in nearby Ann Arbor, formed the group Galen in the 1990s and then joined Couch, the band Galen had opened for at its first show. After moving to Ann Arbor he played with experimental and noise groups including Universal Indians, and co-founded Wolf Eyes, with which he performed until 2004. Late in 2004 he moved to Nepal, where he recorded his own material, field recordings and Nepalese radio broadcasts. He relocated to Ohio in 2007, worked with Emeralds among others, and settled in Oberlin, where he runs the label, record shop and mailorder Hanson Records. His first solo LP, “Modern Jester”, appeared on Hanson Records in 2012, and “The Gag File” followed on Dais Records in 2017. Between the two he kept up a steadier flow of tape releases and collaborative records. Two collaborative albums arrived in 2021: “Lucy & Aaron” with Lucrecia Dalt on Hanson Records, and “Body/Dilloway/Head” with Kim Gordon and Bill Nace’s Body/Head on Three Lobed Recordings. He has also realised John Cage’s 88-tape-loop piece “Rozart Mix” and written an original score for “The Absence of Milk In The Mouths of the Lost”. “No Skill Comedy Mind Reading” is his third solo album and his second for Dais Records, arriving nine years after the last one.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Aaron Dilloway时隔近十年推出的第三张正式个人专辑，素材积累自约十年的创作，以八轨磁带循环、反馈覆盖的拾得声音、田野录音和人声即兴构建而成。他将专辑视为与《Modern Jester》《The Gag File》构成的三部曲终章，试图在极端处境中寻找幽默，笑声采样、低预算恐怖片影响与作曲家Hugo Montenegro遗物中的电子实验笔记共同塑造了不安的段落。磁带嘶声被当作可塑材料而非缺陷，源于他少年时代反复翻录的硬核朋克磁带。整体在刺耳与水下般的闷响之间取得平衡，延续了他将混乱层次转化为独特声响实体的创作路径。

items.body: YZBL Hermaphrodite Feral Crone Recordings It’s tempting to compare recent records by YZBL and Ash Barrett; both take a grimy approach to post-industrial which draws on neighboring heavy and experimental genres, both have seen release on Lana Del Rabies’ new Feral Crone label, and of course, both are the first LPs from former members of stylish Arizona industrial/goth outfit Tassel since its dissolution. But scratch at the rusty patina of any of Hermaphrodite‘s brief pieces and you’ll soon cotton on to YZBL’s modern spin on some classic templates. Hermaphrodite quickly reveals itself as a decidedly rhythmically focused record. Sure, based on YZBL’s Tassel tenure one might read the licks of high feedback guitar which scrape about at the top of “Androgyne”‘s register as classic goth, the record’s overarching undertow draws the ear towards the doomed drony synth, which makes the track feel like a brief precursor to the more explicit pummelling bass of the subsequent “Scissor”. Similarly, the double kicks which seethe pensively at the bottom of “Patterns” end up reframing its sludgy riff, rendering it more controlled and menacing rather than loosely stoned. It’s with all these elements and moods in place that the saturnine shadows of Justin Broadrick and Mick Harris can be felt in the corners of Hermaphrodite. The gruelling crawl of “Piston”, in which serpentine bass weaves its way through rat-trap percussive snaps slow enough for its texture to conjures vintage Godflesh, while the downtempo breaks and dub influences of opener “Lobotomy” and closer “Shinigami” take a page from Scorn. Despite the legacies of these giants, YZBL’s personality is never lost in the record. Both the vocal fragments which are stabbed into the tracks with the same apparent chaos as the guitar feedback – sometimes screamed, sometimes muttered, sometimes heavily distorted, often all of the above as on “Loins” – and her compositional mix of noise, beats, and riffs managing to assemble and dissociate in the span of a couple of minutes keep Hermaphrodite fresh and on edge. Buy it. Hermaphrodite by YZBL The post YZBL, “Hermaphrodite” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以节奏为核心，在黑暗工业声响中融合了高反馈吉他、低沉的无人机合成器与沉重贝斯，呈现出既粗糙又受控的压迫感。开篇的鼓点与贝斯律动带有 dub 影响，缓慢爬行的段落则让人联想到 Godflesh 式的沉重质感，但创作者并未停留在模仿层面。人声碎片以嘶吼、低语和失真处理穿插于乐曲中，与吉他反馈一样具有随机感，使作品在数分钟内不断拆解又重组，保持着紧张与不可预测性。整体上，这是一张在经典工业模板之上注入当代实验思维的专辑，兼具攻击性与细致的声音编排。

items.body: “When you meet a man who is broken, pick him up and carry him. When you meet a woman who’s broken, put her all into your arms. Cause we don’t know where we come from … we don’t know where we are.” -Laurie Anderson Back in college in the early 80’s, my musical tastes careened wildly between the unchecked rage of Dead Kennedys and Black Flag and the deep melancholy of The Cure and Joy Division. (There was an occasional detour to the land of the Talking Heads.) Then my friends and I discovered Laurie Anderson’s Big Science . And everything changed. I think I was the one that found it and that was only because there was a song called Let X=X, which appealed to my math brain. Our first reaction was bewilderment. “What?? She no longer loves the color of my sweaters??!!? Huh??” But we quickly realized this was something new that we needed to absorb. It showed us that we could respond to all the grotesque absurdity of the world with something other than anger or sadness, that it could be met with surrealism and a sense of humor and that we could retain our humanity. We thought about some of the lyrics. On the title track, there’s a lyric: “I think we should put some mountains here. Otherwise what are the characters going to fall off of?” The song is all about how the oligarchs and huge corporations are reshaping the world to their will. They’re building shopping malls and freeways and new sports centres and drive-in banks. They’re reshaping everything for their own self-aggrandisement to the extent that we’re no more than characters in their play, and they even get to decide how we die. We realized this was the same sentiment that Jello Biafra was expressing in so many Dead Kennedys lyrics, just from an entirely different approach. The music was unlike anything we had ever heard before, full of violins, saxophones, marimbas and organs. And was that a wolf? It was beautiful and then jarring at a moment’s notice. Laurie’s voice could sound quite soothing or, when she uses voice processing, terrifying. A few years later, I discovered jazz, especially free jazz and it became an obsession which has lasted to this day. It eventually led me to The Free Jazz Collective. So when I discovered that Laurie was releasing a live album with a jazz band and an excellent one at that, I was extremely excited. The band is Sexmob, consisting of Steven Bernstein and Briggan Krauss on brass, Kenny Wollesen on drums, Douglas Wieselman on winds and guitar, and Tony Scherr on bass. They have an extensive discography which is well worth checking out. They like covering pop songs, and giving them an avant-garde jazz twist. I especially love Kenny Wolleson who I’ve seen perform many times, frequently in John Zorn projects. The album, called Let X=X (Live), is full of the classics that every Laurie Anderson fan knows note for note and lyric for lyric, From The Air, O Superman, Let X=X, It Tango, Gravity’s Angel, Only An Expert , and on and on. But there’s new music to be found here as well. Church of Panic begins with a commentary on sadness and suicide and then turns on a dime and is funky as hell. There are lovely instrumental pieces like Looking At The Mo on. There’s an extremely funny (and at the same time sad) audience participation moment on Teachers which I won’t spoil. Junior Dad , from Lou Reed’s collaboration with Metallica, features Reed’s vocals with beautiful violin from Laurie. There is quite a bit of sadness on this album at the state of the world and at all of the personal loss so many have suffered lately, but there is also an ember of hope to be found. It’s a hope that humanity might someday soon rediscover its compassion and decency. It’s a sky-blue sky. Let X=X (Live) by Laurie Anderson Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张现场专辑是 Laurie Anderson 与爵士乐团 SexMob 的合作，重新演绎了她八十年代以来的经典曲目，如《O Superman》《Let X=X》《Gravity's Angel》等。SexMob 以铜管、木管、打击乐和贝斯构建起自由即兴的骨架，在保留原作超现实主义文本与政治讽喻的同时，用爵士乐的松散与张力重塑了电子声效、提琴和合成器营造的怪异美感。Anderson 的人声在温和与经过处理器扭曲之间切换，与乐队的爆发力形成对话。乐评回溯了这些作品当年如何以荒诞幽默回应世界性的荒谬，并指出爵士版本的演绎既忠实于原曲的情感内核，又赋予其现场呼吸的流动性。整张专辑呈现出实验声乐与自由爵士碰撞的独特质感，值得深入聆听。

items.body:
“The thing about playing the tuba in an orchestra is that you don’t have to play that much,” admitted composer Matthew Wright, who grew up playing the tuba in orchestras and funk bands, “but it’s the best seat in the house. You hear music back to front. The percussion and the brass are loud, so you hear all their detail, and the strings are this kind of ethereal thing that’s off in the distance.”

For the Kent-based Wright, who also improvises using turntables, samplers, and processers – most impactfully with Trance Map, his partnership with Evan Parker – this early realization nurtured a sensibility leading to the creation of immersive works that mix composition, improvisation, and technology. Cracked Glaze (False Walls) is a case in point, as it utilizes notated material – “dot music” is his good-humored term – improvisation, and Wright’s real-time sampling and processing immediately fed into surround sound, all of which he remixed for the CD.

Wright’s collaborators on Cracked Glaze represent various facets of his work. Ensemble Klang, an ensemble of mostly Dutch new music virtuosi, was an early champion of Wright’s compositions. Spheric Totemic is a Wright-instigated, flexibly configured improvising group with, on this occasion, Mandhira de Saram, Alexander Hawkins, Neil Charles and Stephen Davis. Sofia Jernberg, whose Musho with Hawkins was one of the brighter lights of 2024, is new to Wright’s constellation.

Historically, the conventional wisdom among exponents of freely improvised music is that the larger the group, the more apt the music will be muddied. It is a yardstick that is also prevalent among practitioners of contemporary composition. Individuality – of the improviser, of the composer – is more difficult to assert in or through a crowd. Although there are more than a dozen musicians heard on Cracked Glaze, there is no nebulous sprawl or complexity for complexity’s sake. Abstraction is tethered to figuration, the spine of the piece being a descending line that repeatedly submerges and reemerges, giving the interactions of voices clear relationships.

“In a lot of my written work for ensembles there is a central concern that tends to last a long period of time, an idea that will give the piece structure. I’m really interested in music being a kind of terrain that you can hear through and around, so that when you are listening, you are experiencing a kind of ‘visual’ situation. I guess this goes back to my work with vinyl records, because records make music a physical surface, where you can place the needle anywhere in the terrain of the music.

“In the improvised work, I don’t want to be the guy that says to improvisers, ‘this is how it goes.’ Improvisation, in a free context, is about distributed leadership. It’s about this beautiful situation of people saying, ‘the music could go here’ or ‘I hear the future of this music in what you’re playing,’ and the kind of listening that leads to those sorts of situations.

“Having the opportunity to work with a group that is mainly readers – Ensemble Klang – and a group that is mainly improvisers – Spheric Totemic – and Sofia Jernberg, gave me the opportunity to do something I haven’t done much of in my music, to have a spine that is unfurling but is always there. It doesn’t necessarily always have to be the main focus of the piece, but it will always be there. It will structure time in a certain way; improvisers can do whatever they want to do, and the music will be as much about them as it is the spine. I was really interested in having a sort of ‘object’ in the space of the improvisation. It’s almost like in the visual art world, where you have people moving around in a gallery but there’s a sculpture there. It’s in the room with you.”

Another virtue of Cracked Glaze is that it is the type of work that initially seems to come out of nowhere. It smacks of singularity. However, Wright’s backstory reveals that he did not come out of nowhere, as he has a pedigree linking him to England’s most consequential institutional incubator of experimental music, as well as its most venerable, living exponent of improvised music. Both associations largely account for how Wright’s disparate interests – several of which were common among Gen Xers in their formative years but were delayed in being assimilated into experimental music – were shaped into a mature aesthetic, and yielded in Cracked Glaze an arguably definitive statement.

“My experience, first of all, was writing music and playing in brass bands and funk bands and small improvising groups with friends,” Wright recently explained. “But I also liked writing chamber music for people who would take it away and play it somewhere else. I might not even be there for the performance. This background took me to study at the University of Huddersfield with the Professor who set up the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival, Richard Steinitz. I was very lucky. It was kind of random. He was my composition teacher. So, I was very lucky to have experiences like knocking on the door for a composition lesson and Richard Steinitz saying, ‘Ah, Matt, I can’t possibly teach you right now, but meet Karlheinz,’ and the door opens and there’s this world-famous composer from another generation that I had read about, but never dreamed I would meet.

“Contemporary classical music was a big part of my education, but I DJed as a kid. I was really interested at that point in the ‘80s and ‘90s when software, sampling, and DJ technology, was becoming affordable. It started showing up in people’s homes. Contemporary classical music and DJ culture were colliding in my mind when I was a kid. The only kind of formal education I could get was a classical education, along with some jazz theory, but it was largely based on dot music, written music. Then there was this other (non-written) side, like DJ culture and all of the great heritage of Black music that DJ culture is part of, and that was a kind of informal education I studied for myself.

“When I was a real little kid – like 12 or 13 – I made a lot of bedroom productions with a basic computer and turntable setup, really focused on instrumental hip-hop. I started to scratch around then, just watching how it was done on TV. My main inspirations were DJ Premier of Gangstarr, Terminator X of Public Enemy, and Maseo of De La Soul. When I was around 18 or 19, as a student, I DJed for a few parties, playing mainly funk, hip hop, and drum ‘n' bass. Around the same time – 1996-98 – I was in a few pop/funk bands that needed a DJ, so I did a few things with beat juggling and matching the pitch of the horns with turntable scratches, etc.

“In 1999 I DJed for a social event at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival and I decided to just play fragments of music that I loved at the time: The Jazz Warriors, Louis Andriessen, Loose Tubes, Squarepusher, Björk. On the basis of that weird mix, I got the call to DJ at Abbey Road for the launch of a music charity, the PRS Foundation, in 2000. That was both a social event and included some (not entirely successful!) experimental scratching. When I moved to Holland to study with composer Louis Andriessen in 2002, I joined a trio with laptop artist Tom Tlalim and saxophonist Keir Neuringer – now of Irreversible Entanglements – and we played a few house parties and small gigs with our own mix of free improv and beat-based electronica. That same year the Huddersfield Festival commissioned ‘Presents from an Edited Then’ which was a 70-minute piece for The Apollo Saxophone Quartet and me DJing, designed for a club venue, again a mix of ‘social’ and ‘experimental’. That’s when I got interested in the worlds of contemporary classical music and DJ culture colliding.”

One of the first projects Wright embarked on was to compose for turntables and to teach classically-trained percussionists how to use them, integrating John Cage’s early work for percussion with the innovations of Christian Marclay and Otomo Yoshihide. “In a piece called Contact Theatre I had literally written out all of the material for notation-reading percussionists”, Wright said of the work. “If you look at a musical stave with the four spaces between the lines, I used those spaces to represent the four spaces on a vinyl record. The space that would be a F in the treble stave, that’s the space on the outer edge of the record, before any musical material appears on the vinyl record. All of the musical material on the record is included in the second space, and then the space at the center of the record was the third space, and then the label itself in the fourth space. You can prepare those spaces, put stickers on them. I would literally write percussion rhythms and they could produce those rhythms by dropping the needle on the record and get a ricochet effect or specify a section of the record I want to be played, say a saxophone solo three minutes into the record. I developed these ‘half-contact’ techniques where the needle sticks like a locked groove, and I taught the basics of hip hop scratching to percussionists, even though the music didn’t sound anything like hip hop.”

Wright then began to assess the proportions of and the relationships between the elements of his aesthetic and how to integrate them in his work. “Cracked Glaze is a collision of all of the above. I have been doing ensemble work and turntable work and installation work, but a lot of my focus is on the work with Evan in mixing and even post-production of the Trance Map material. Post-production is really part of the process, and Evan is very interested in exploring all that. Although Cracked Glaze doesn’t involve Evan, it brings to equal terms all of the sources I work with. There’s some notation written for Ensemble Klang with holes in that notation, space for the improvisation group of Spheric Totemic and Sofia Jernberg. They have start and stop times for the improvising, and they also sometimes have cues for some notation. I’m also mixing them live on stage, taking samples and remixing them and using the turntable as well. Then I take all that material and work on it a little in the studio, not to radically change the piece but to bring out some of the elements that you would hear live but not in a stereo recording. The piece brings together notation, improvisation, and technology, but not as separate forms. They all intersect. That’s where they all join on the map.”

In a roundabout way, the title of the piece speaks to the processes of its creation. It refers to the glazes used in high-fire ceramics that are formulated to crack on temperature; even though they are applied in an even manner, the cracking results in a surface that can be likened to a mosaic assembled with random tiles, with dark, hair-thin spaces between them. Though the results are subject to a unique firing, the experienced artist knows how to promote cracking that is pleasing and avoid cracking that ruins the piece.

“It may be interesting to talk about how jazz standards have worked in the past,” Wright responded to the idea of controlled cracking, and chuckling at the notion that he controlled the gas valve. “An excellent standard is one that can be played in its entirety and feel integrated and beautiful, but it is also a catalyst. It offers itself up to be cracked, to be turned into something new. In some ways, the use of notation to suggest a response is fascinating to me. On a technical level, there are definitely moments where I say to the improvisers, ‘at a certain point you will hear a line and at that point, that pitch, that’s your moment; if you’re improvising, the natural ebb and flow of the group will go to you’. But I don’t say ‘you should crack it’ to them; I say ‘it’s yours’.

“And there’s a third element there, the equivalent of the heat – the processing and the spatialization. I’m taking the feed of everybody, the notated music and the improvised music is coming to my setup, and I’m able to remix it and sample it. I’m an agent in the cracking, too. Whether it is notated or not is not the point, because it’s all going through the same system and being splintered into surround sound. That’s the third element, the sound design is a catalytic element.”

Wright pointed to a poster in his studio of a still influential Japanese textile exhibition he attended in his early 20s. “What I loved about that,” he said, “was that the dynamic shapes of these textiles are very rigid, spatially, but the textiles themselves have all sorts of holes in them. They are almost like fishing nets. I tried to create something similar by creating a structure that’s flexible but has holes in it. If we play this piece again, the melody line and the structure is going to be exactly the same every time and the improvising and the specialization will be different every time. That’s a long-winded way of saying I tried not to over notate.”

Wright acknowledged that post-production, particularly when the work was created in a surround sound environment and is remixed for stereo, creates a distinct experience of the work, and perhaps represents a new iteration of the pursuit of perfection in the studio, exemplified by Glenn Gould. “My pieces are concepts that have a sort of quantum existence,” Wright maintained. “What I mean is that if we are going to present the piece live, then there are circumstances that will be dynamic for the audience in the live space that may not be so dynamic when hearing it at home. In the live space, I’m dealing with surround sound. There are a whole lot of options to try to present that sort of experience in the stereo format. When it comes to making a CD or something online that people will listen to, I consider the domestic setting. I also consider that many people listen to music on the go, with headphones or their phone. You may be walking down the Avenue of the Americas and everything around you is changing, but there’s one consistent thread in the music.

“You have to consider the multiple ways that people listen now. I do hope that people will sit at home to listen to it. In that situation, it’s much closer to reading a book because it’s a solitary experience. You’re sitting with it for 40 or 50 minutes. Wearing headphones creates an interior experience. I really treasure those kinds of listeners and it’s a real privilege when someone spends that time with something that I’ve made with my musical friends.

“In the history of improvised music there have been many vehement statements about the relationship between free improvised music and recording. I totally get that, but I suppose that the question we now have to consider is what happens when you improvise with a recording. We don’t want the karaoke thing! How does the recording come back into the improvised music experience in as fluid a way you would have with another musician with an instrument? An instrument is obviously a technology of its own and the recording is the result of the technology. We need to make sure the technology is as flexible as any other instrument. The other thing I’m really fascinated by in the history of free creative music is the evolution of incorporating electronics. It’s really interesting for me when an electro-acoustic improvised situation might suggest that the music is not happening in the present tense, but in the past or the future.

“The thing I’m really interested in is those previously separated camps of notation, improvisation, and technology becoming one and the same, where there is an equaling out of the three. You’re not relying on one form of expression. And this seems to be causing a real revitalization of the scene, where people are mastering their separate disciplines and are also negotiating with each other. I think there’s more opportunity for creative music because of the dialogue between notation, improvisation, and technology. Looking for the connections between them is the main creative impetus. It’s not paper; it’s not technology; it’s not adherence to one way of making music. It’s about thinking about the connections between the people you’re working with. Saying ‘all of the above’ may be too easy an answer, but it does ascribe equal value to notation, improvisation and technology. These are all zones on the map and they all overlap each other, so the paths between those zones are what I’m interested in.”

***

Wright’s projects frequently overlap, the post production of one coinciding with the development of another. With summer approaching, Wright was mixing a duo session with Pat Thomas that has the flavor of This is Trickster; a Spheric Totemic album, and a Trance Map + recording on which Parker and him are joined by harpist Milana Zaric and Richard Barrett.

The presence of Barrett is particularly intriguing, as he pioneered improvised electronic music beginning in the 1990s – largely through FURT, his partnership with Paul Obermayer – laying groundwork for Wright and others. Additionally, Barrett’s compositions are renowned for testing – and often surpassing – the presumed physical limits of instrumentalists.

Barrett and Wright are part of a trajectory of composers foregrounding technology in their work. An earlier dot on the line, one that is essential but not obvious, is Conlon Nancarrow. The expatriate composer is the inspiration for Wright’s next major work, “Passing Nancarrow.” Wright’s latest project with the Belgian ensemble BL!NDMAN (the exclamation point is intentional) also has Hawkins in a key role. The piece debuts next year, marking 30 years since Nancarrow died.

“The idea of the piece is based around Nancarrow being obsessed with Art Tatum’s playing,” Wright explained. “He sampled Tatum in the form of piano rolls, using technology from a hundred years ago. What we will do is, while Alex improvises in real time, his notes are captured and this will trigger all sorts of reactions from the group. In a way, we turn Alex’s music into a piano roll.”

Wright was partly inspired by the writer and documentary film director Helen Borton’s comment that jazz and blues collide like a “hurricane” in Nancarrow’s music. Replace “hurricane” with “Nancarrow” and you get the gist of Wright’s conceptualization for the recording he is currently mixing – “four hurricanes of all kinds of crazy sounds.” Wright also considered the music of Squarepusher, Aphex Twin, and other exponents of electronic dance music, that influenced him when Nancarrow died in 1997, leading him to include “strange, intelligent dance music in the piece.”

However, the nexus of Nancarrow, Barrett, and Wright, is the consideration of the limits of music humans can create in real time, and how to get to the edge of those limits, if not extend them.

“Nancarrow reached for impossible, post-human music. But in my current work, I don’t have an artistic interest in post-human AI. I’ve heard a lot of AI-generated music and read a lot of AI research, and the thing I’m already bored by is that AI can do almost anything. Like a musician that can play everything and just won’t stop playing to give space for others, AI doing anything and everything is boring to me when you don’t hear inspired choices and you don’t hear the human labor or the human need for considered space in the music. But, I’m open minded. I just haven’t heard anything that inspires me yet. Back to the human level, in Alex’s piano playing, there is that reaching beyond what is supposedly humanly possible, to reach a new vista for what is possible.

“You can say that, for his times, Nancarrow was making a post-human kind of music, but we should remember that he sat there, punching holes. So, I don’t hear a sort of pre-AI in his music, a piano that can do anything, but the blood and the hours of Nancarrow sitting maybe six months to create an explosive two minutes. I want to know how humans feel when they hear music and when they make music. If that is aided by technology, the idea is that the technology helps musical thinking like an instrument helps musical thinking. My interest in technology is the same as Alex’s interest in the piano, there’s a tradition of human tool use there that in a sense heightens the human listening experience if done successfully.

“Another thing I like about Nancarrow was that he was true to his beliefs, which is why he left the US for Mexico City, which resulted in him working in relative isolation. He just got on with it. A few people had experimented with the player piano before, but he made it his own. I appreciate that you can hear the edges in music and you’re OK with not being able to know everything beyond that edge. I guess the difference between the scene we have now and Nancarrow’s situation is that we can go to the edge together in a collaborative spirit.”
